title: Removing Duplicates and Splitting Text
summary: Clean your Orders data by removing duplicate rows, split combined text into separate columns, and write formulas that reference cells on other sheets.

steps.title: Removing Duplicate Rows Permanently
steps.lede: When the same order number appears twice in your Orders sheet, Excel's Remove Duplicates tool clears the extras — but the deletion is permanent.

blocks.text: Say the same order number shows up twice in your Orders sheet — maybe it was entered once by mistake. Excel has a dedicated tool for this, but it's worth being careful with.
When you use the Remove Duplicates feature, the duplicate data is permanently deleted, so it's a good idea to copy the original data to another worksheet before removing duplicates.

To remove duplicates, select the range of cells that has duplicate values, select Data > Remove Duplicates, and then check or uncheck the columns under Columns to choose which columns are used to identify a duplicate row. On your Orders sheet, checking only the order_id column means two rows with the same order number get treated as duplicates even if other columns differ — while checking every column would only catch rows that match everywhere.

annotations.text: LG-2005 — duplicate removed; row count reduced by 1

blocks.change_summary: Remove Duplicates on the order_id column deleted the second LG-2005 row permanently.

segments.label: Copy data first, then remove duplicates by all columns or a single column
segments.summary: The presenter works with a sales table (Sales Agent, Region, Sales Value) and explains that a duplicate is only a duplicate when every selected column matches — two rows with the same agent but different sales values are not duplicates. Before running the tool, she copies the entire table to a separate area so the original is preserved. She then clicks inside the data, opens Data > Data Tools > Remove Duplicates, confirms the headers checkbox and all columns are selected, and clicks OK — Excel reports five duplicates removed and 14 unique rows remain. She repeats the process on the Sales Agent column alone, this time deselecting the other columns, and the result is a distinct list of four agents with 15 duplicates removed.

bridge.before: Watch how the Columns checklist controls which rows count as duplicates, and notice the copy step before any deletion.
bridge.after: The clip uses 'Sales Agent' as its example column; the same logic applies to any key column, such as an order-number column.

steps.title: Permanent Deletion and the Copy Precaution
steps.lede: Confirm you understand what Remove Duplicates does to your data.

public.prompt: You are about to use Data > Remove Duplicates on your Orders sheet. Which statement best describes what you should do before running it, and why?

options.text: Copy the original data to another worksheet first, because Remove Duplicates permanently deletes the duplicate rows and the deletion cannot be undone once the workbook is saved and closed.
Sort the data by order_id first, because Remove Duplicates only works correctly on sorted data.
No preparation is needed; Remove Duplicates moves duplicates to a separate sheet so you can review them later.
Apply a filter to hide blank rows first, because Remove Duplicates will treat blank rows as duplicates and delete them.

opt_b.message: Remove Duplicates does not require sorted data. It compares rows based on the columns you select, regardless of their order in the sheet.

opt_c.message: Remove Duplicates does not move rows to another sheet — it permanently deletes them from the current sheet. There is no built-in review step.

opt_d.message: Remove Duplicates identifies duplicate rows based on the column values you select, not on whether rows are blank. Filtering blank rows first is not required and does not protect your original data.

correct.message: Correct! Remove Duplicates permanently deletes the duplicate rows. Copying the original data to another worksheet before running it gives you a backup in case you need to recover any rows.

incorrect.message: Remove Duplicates permanently deletes duplicate rows — there is no undo once the workbook is saved. The recommended precaution is to copy the original data to another worksheet before running the operation.

hints: Think about what 'permanently deleted' means for your data if you make a mistake.
The key word in the fact is 'permanently' — what safety step does that suggest?

steps.title: Configure and Run Remove Duplicates
steps.lede: Select the correct columns to identify duplicate rows in the Orders sheet and run the tool.

public.prompt: The Orders table has order IDs in column A (A2:A21). When you run Data > Remove Duplicates and select only the **order_id** column in the Columns checklist, Excel compares rows using only that column. Type a formula in cell B1 that returns the order ID from the first data row (A2), confirming you can reference the cleaned data.

correct.message: Correct! =A2 returns 'LG-2001', the order ID in the first data row. After running Remove Duplicates on the order_id column, only unique order IDs remain — each row is identified by a distinct order ID.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell A2 directly. The order ID in the first data row is in cell A2 of the Orders sheet.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The first data row is row 2 (row 1 is the header). The order_id column is column A.

steps.title: Splitting One Column into Two
steps.lede: When a single cell holds combined text like "Lagos,Nigeria", Text to Columns splits it into separate columns using a delimiter you choose.

blocks.text: To split text into columns, select the cell or column that contains the text, select Data > Text to Columns, choose Delimited, select the delimiter(s) such as Comma or Space, choose the destination for the split data, and select Finish. If your Orders sheet has a single column holding "Lagos,Nigeria" as one text value, running Text to Columns with Comma as the delimiter splits it into two columns.

annotations.text: Last Name — split by Space delimiter

blocks.change_summary: Text to Columns with Space delimiter split the Full Name column into First Name and Last Name.

segments.label: Splitting a full-name column into separate columns using Text to Columns
segments.summary: Starting from a single column of full names, the demonstrator opens the Data tab, clicks Text to Columns, selects Delimited, then checks Space as the delimiter. The data preview immediately shows a dividing line between first and last names. Clicking Finish splits the column into two. The presenter also notes that other characters—such as a comma or a custom symbol—can be entered in the Other field to serve as the delimiter instead.

steps.title: Split a Delimited Column
steps.lede: Choose the correct steps to split a comma-delimited column using Text to Columns.

public.prompt: Column B of your Orders sheet contains entries like 'Lagos,Nigeria' — city and country combined in a single cell, separated by a comma. You want to split this into two separate columns. Which sequence of steps correctly uses Text to Columns to do this?

options.text: Select column B, choose Data > Text to Columns, select Delimited, check Comma as the delimiter, choose the destination, and select Finish.
Select column B, choose Data > Text to Columns, select Fixed Width, drag a break line between the city and country, and select Finish.
Select column B, choose Home > Find & Replace, enter ',' in Find, leave Replace blank, and select Replace All.
Select column B, choose Data > Remove Duplicates, check the Comma delimiter option, and select OK.

opt_b.message: Fixed Width is used when columns are separated by a consistent number of characters (like a fixed-width export), not by a delimiter character. Since the separator here is a comma, choose Delimited instead.

opt_c.message: Find & Replace removes or replaces text but does not split a cell into two columns. You need Text to Columns to distribute the split values into separate columns.

opt_d.message: Remove Duplicates removes repeated rows — it has nothing to do with splitting cell contents. Use Data > Text to Columns for splitting.

correct.message: Correct! Data > Text to Columns > Delimited > Comma splits 'Lagos,Nigeria' into two separate columns. The destination setting controls where the split values are placed.

incorrect.message: To split a column by a delimiter character (like a comma), use Data > Text to Columns, choose Delimited, select the delimiter (Comma), set the destination, and click Finish.

hints: The key word is 'delimited' — the data uses a specific character (comma) to separate the parts.
Text to Columns is on the Data tab, not the Home tab.

steps.title: Split the Full Name Column
steps.lede: Use Data > Text to Columns with Space as the delimiter to split the driver name column into First Name and Last Name.

public.prompt: The location column (column B) in this Orders table stores city and country as a single value separated by a comma, for example 'Lagos,Nigeria'. After running Data > Text to Columns with Comma as the delimiter, the city part would move to column B and the country part to column C. Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the current combined value from B2, confirming you can read the source data before splitting.

correct.message: Correct! =B2 returns 'Lagos,Nigeria' — the combined city and country value in the first data row. After running Text to Columns with Comma as the delimiter, this cell would contain only 'Lagos' and the next column would contain 'Nigeria'.

incorrect.message: Type a formula that references cell B2. The location column is column B, and the first data row is row 2.

hints: A formula that returns the value from another cell starts with = followed by the cell address.
The location column is column B; the first data row is row 2.

steps.title: Referencing Cells on Another Sheet
steps.lede: A formula on your Orders sheet can pull a value directly from your Drivers sheet — or even from a different workbook — using a cross-sheet reference.

blocks.text: A formula can refer to a cell on another sheet in the same workbook by writing the sheet name followed by an exclamation point (!) and then the cell or range reference, for example Marketing!B1. So a formula on your Orders sheet that needs a value sitting on your Drivers sheet could reference Drivers!B1.

If the referenced worksheet's name contains spaces or numbers, the name must be enclosed in single quotation marks in the reference, for example ='January Revenue'!A1. So if you renamed your drivers tab to "Driver List", a reference to it would need to be written 'Driver List'!A1, not Driver List!A1.

A workbook link to a cell range in another workbook, when the source workbook is open, includes the workbook name in square brackets, followed by the worksheet name, an exclamation point, and the cells the formula depends on, for example =SUM([Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25).

blocks.title: Cross-Sheet Reference Syntax

nodes.label: Sheet name (no spaces, no quotes needed)
Single quotes required when name contains space
Square brackets around external workbook name

blocks.alt_text: Formula bar showing cross-sheet reference syntax. Three examples: Drivers!B1 (simple reference with sheet name, exclamation point, and cell address), 'January Revenue'!A1 (single quotes wrap sheet names containing spaces), and [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10 (square brackets contain external workbook name).

steps.title: Same-Workbook and Cross-Workbook References
steps.lede: Choose the correct reference syntax for same-workbook and cross-workbook scenarios.

public.prompt: You are on the Summary sheet and need to pull a value from cell B1 on the Drivers sheet in the same workbook. Which formula is correct?

opt_b.message: A dot (.) is not the separator between a sheet name and a cell reference. The correct separator is an exclamation point (!), giving Drivers!B1.

opt_c.message: Square brackets are used for workbook names in cross-workbook links (e.g., [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10), not for sheet names within the same workbook.

opt_d.message: A colon (:) is used to define a range (e.g., A1:B5), not to separate a sheet name from a cell reference. Use an exclamation point (!) instead.

correct.message: Correct! Within the same workbook, a cross-sheet reference uses the sheet name followed by an exclamation point and the cell address: Drivers!B1.

incorrect.message: A cross-sheet reference within the same workbook uses the sheet name, an exclamation point (!), and the cell address — for example, Drivers!B1. Square brackets are reserved for cross-workbook links.

hints: The separator between a sheet name and a cell address is the exclamation point (!).
Square brackets [ ] appear only in cross-workbook links, not in same-workbook references.

steps.title: Choosing the Right Reference Syntax
steps.lede: Given a formula requirement, select the correctly formed cross-sheet reference.

public.prompt: You need to write a formula on the Summary sheet that sums cells C10:C25 from a sheet named 'Annual' inside a separate open workbook called Budget.xlsx. Which formula is correct?

opt_b.message: The workbook name must be enclosed in square brackets, not followed by an exclamation point directly. The correct syntax is [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25.

opt_c.message: Single quotes are used to enclose sheet names that contain spaces or numbers, not workbook file names. The workbook name goes in square brackets: [Budget.xlsx].

opt_d.message: This formula references the Annual sheet in the current workbook, not in Budget.xlsx. To reference another workbook, include the workbook name in square brackets before the sheet name.

correct.message: Correct! A cross-workbook link uses the workbook name in square brackets, followed by the sheet name, an exclamation point, and the cell range: [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25.

incorrect.message: A cross-workbook link (when the source workbook is open) uses the format [WorkbookName.xlsx]SheetName!CellRange. The workbook name goes in square brackets, not in quotes or with an extra exclamation point.

hints: Cross-workbook links have three parts: [workbook name], sheet name, and cell range — in that order.
Square brackets [ ] wrap the workbook file name; single quotes wrap sheet names that contain spaces.

steps.title: Write a Cross-Sheet Reference
steps.lede: Write a formula in cell B2 of a Summary sheet that pulls the value from cell B4 on a sheet named Q1 Sales.

public.prompt:
The workbook contains a sheet named **'2024Q1'** (the name starts with a number). In cell Z1 of the current sheet, write a formula that pulls the value from cell B4 on the '2024Q1' sheet.

Remember: when a sheet name starts with a number (or contains a space), it must be enclosed in single quotation marks in the reference.

tests.message_on_fail: Z1 should return 'Lagos' (the city in row 4 of the 2024Q1 sheet). Make sure you quote the sheet name: ='2024Q1'!B4

correct.message: Well done! ='2024Q1'!B4 correctly references cell B4 on the '2024Q1' sheet. The single quotes around the sheet name are required because the name starts with a number.

incorrect.message: The formula should be ='2024Q1'!B4. The sheet name '2024Q1' must be enclosed in single quotes because it starts with a number. Without the quotes, the spreadsheet cannot parse the reference.

hints: The syntax for a cross-sheet reference is SheetName!CellAddress. When the sheet name starts with a number (or has a space), wrap it in single quotes.
Try typing ='2024Q1'!B4 — the single quotes go around the entire sheet name, before the exclamation point.

steps.title: Cleaning, Splitting, and Linking — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now remove duplicate rows safely, split delimited text into columns, and reference cells across sheets.

blocks.text: Remove Duplicates permanently deletes matched rows — copy your data first. Choose which columns define a duplicate: checking only order_id catches same-ID rows even if other columns differ. Text to Columns splits a delimited column in three steps: choose Delimited, pick the delimiter (Comma, Space, or other), then Finish. Cross-sheet references use the syntax SheetName!CellAddress; if the sheet name contains spaces or numbers, wrap it in single quotes: 'Sheet Name'!A1. Cross-workbook links add the workbook name in square brackets: [Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10.

blocks.title: Next: Formula Syntax and References
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll write formulas with arithmetic operators, understand operator precedence, and lock cells with absolute references using the $ sign.

remediation_steps.title: Why Copy Before Removing Duplicates
remediation_steps.lede: See the contrast between a reversible and an irreversible operation.

blocks.text: Sorting your Orders sheet is reversible — you can sort again in a different order. Remove Duplicates is not: once you click OK, the matched rows are gone and there is no undo after you save. Copying the sheet to a backup tab first means you can always recover the original rows if you removed too many. The copy step takes seconds; recovering without it can be impossible.

remediation_steps.title: Text to Columns: The Three Steps
remediation_steps.lede: Walk through the wizard steps one more time with a concrete example.

blocks.text: Starting from a column that holds "Lagos,Nigeria" in each cell: (1) select the column, (2) click Data > Text to Columns, (3) choose Delimited and click Next, (4) check Comma as the delimiter — the preview shows the split — (5) choose a destination cell and click Finish. The single column becomes two: one with "Lagos" and one with "Nigeria". Choosing Space instead of Comma would split on the space character instead.

remediation_steps.title: Cross-Sheet vs. Cross-Workbook Syntax
remediation_steps.lede: Compare the two reference forms side by side.

blocks.text: Same workbook, simple sheet name: Drivers!B1 — sheet name, exclamation point, cell address. Same workbook, sheet name with a space: 'January Revenue'!A1 — single quotes wrap the name. Different workbook (source open): =SUM([Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25) — workbook name in square brackets before the sheet name. The square brackets only appear for cross-workbook links; within the same workbook you never use them.

remediation_steps.title: When Do Sheet Names Need Quotes?
remediation_steps.lede: The quoting rule is simple: any name that contains a space or a number needs single quotes.

blocks.text: Drivers!B1 — no quotes needed; the name has no spaces or numbers. 'January Revenue'!A1 — quotes required; the name contains a space. '2024 Orders'!C5 — quotes required; the name contains a number. Forgetting the quotes when they're needed causes a formula error. A safe habit: always click the sheet tab while typing the formula and let Excel insert the correct syntax automatically.
